marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q001.takeaway: Epidermal layers are ordered from superficial to deep as corneum, granulosum, spinosum and basale; thick skin adds lucidum.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q001.displayText: The image is a histological section of epidermis. The marked layers correspond to stratum corneum, stratum granulosum, stratum spinosum, and stratum basale; therefore option D gives the correct mapping. Thin hairy skin has these four layers. Thick glabrous skin of palms and soles additionally has a clear stratum lucidum between stratum corneum and stratum granulosum.

rationales.a: This assigns the markers to the wrong layers: the key maps A-2, B-1, C-3 and D-4.
rationales.b: This swaps marker B/C relative to the source map and misassigns the basal/corneal layers.
rationales.c: This changes the source-keyed B-1 and D-4 layer assignments; the ordered map is A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q002.takeaway: Stratum spinosum is the prickle-cell layer because keratinocytes remain attached at desmosomes during tissue preparation.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q002.displayText: Stratum spinosum is the prickle-cell layer. Its keratinocytes are attached by desmosomes. During H&E preparation the cells shrink away from one another except at these attachments, making the desmosomes appear as spines or prickles.

rationales.a: Stratum basale is the deepest epidermal layer, not the prickle-cell layer.
rationales.c: Stratum granulosum is superficial to the spinosum and contains keratohyalin granules; the prickle appearance is at spinosum desmosomes.
rationales.d: Stratum corneum is the outer keratinized layer, not the desmosome-rich prickle-cell layer.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q003.takeaway: The stratum corneum contains multiple layers of flattened, anucleate keratinocytes.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q003.displayText: Stratum corneum is composed of multiple layers of flattened, anucleate, keratinized cells that can intertwine. Keratinocytes originate in the stratum basale and progressively lose their nuclei and dehydrate as they migrate superficially. The thick stratum corneum contributes to the epidermal barrier against microbes and fluid loss.

rationales.a: Stratum lucidum is the clear layer present only in thick skin; the multiple intertwining anucleate layers form the corneum.
rationales.b: Stratum basale contains proliferating keratinocytes with nuclei, not the superficial anucleate layers.
rationales.c: Stratum granulosum contains granular keratinocytes, but the fully flattened anucleate cells are in the stratum corneum.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q004.takeaway: Desmosomes are cell-to-cell adhesive junctions that resist shearing in the epidermis.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q004.displayText: The marked region points to intercellular adhesions formed by desmosomes. Desmosomes (maculae adherentes) are adhesive junctions that maintain mechanical integrity and resist shearing. They include desmosomal cadherins, cytoplasmic plaque proteins such as plakoglobin/plakophilin/desmoplakin, and keratin intermediate filaments. Hemidesmosomes instead mediate cell-to-extracellular-matrix adhesion.

rationales.a: Melanocytes are pigment-producing basal cells, not the intercellular junction marked in the epidermis.
rationales.b: Sweat-gland ducts traverse the skin but are not the cell-to-cell junction identified as desmosomes.
rationales.d: Hemidesmosomes attach basal cells to basement membrane; the marked cell-to-cell adhesion is a desmosome.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q005.takeaway: Psoriasis elongates and clubs the epidermal rete ridges (epidermal pegs).
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q005.displayText: The clinical picture is psoriasis. The marked structures are epidermal pegs (rete ridges), downward projections of epidermis between dermal papillae. Psoriasis characteristically shows elongation and clubbing of rete ridges.

rationales.a: Reticular dermis is connective tissue beneath the papillary dermis; psoriasis elongates epidermal rete ridges.
rationales.b: Hair follicles are epithelial invaginations associated with hair, not the clubbed epidermal pegs described in psoriasis.
rationales.c: Papillary dermis forms upward projections between rete ridges; the marked downward epidermal projections are epidermal pegs.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q006.takeaway: Melanocytes occupy the stratum basale and transfer melanin to keratinocytes.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q006.displayText: Melanocytes are located in the stratum basale. They are neural-crest-derived cells that migrate to the basal epidermis during development. They synthesize melanin in melanosomes and transfer it through dendritic processes to surrounding keratinocytes.

rationales.a: Melanocytes are not located in the outer anucleate stratum corneum.
rationales.b: Stratum granulosum is above the basal layer; melanocytes reside in the stratum basale.
rationales.d: The epidermal melanocytes are specifically in the basal layer, not the underlying dermis.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q007.takeaway: Merkel cells are slowly adapting light-touch mechanoreceptors in the basal epidermis.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q007.displayText: Merkel cells are slow-adapting mechanoreceptors involved in light touch. They are found in the stratum basale of highly sensitive skin, including fingertips and around hair follicles, and are contacted by unmyelinated sensory nerve endings.

rationales.a: Melanocytes synthesize melanin; they are not the slowly adapting touch receptors.
rationales.b: Keratinocytes form most of the epidermis but are not the Merkel touch-receptor cells.
rationales.c: Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting immune cells, not the slow-adapting mechanoreceptors.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q008.takeaway: Pacinian corpuscles are onion-like, rapidly adapting receptors for pressure and vibration.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q008.displayText: The marked structure is a Pacinian corpuscle. It is a large onion-like receptor in the dermis and hypodermis, made of concentric lamellae of flattened Schwann cells and collagen around an axon. It is a rapidly adapting mechanoreceptor for coarse touch, pressure and vibration.

rationales.a: Merkel cells mediate sustained fine touch in the basal epidermis; the marked large lamellar receptor is Pacinian.
rationales.b: Meissner corpuscles are smaller receptors in papillary dermis for light touch, not the large onion-like corpuscle marked here.
rationales.d: Ruffini endings detect skin stretch and are not the concentric lamellar pressure/vibration receptor shown.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q009.takeaway: Meissner corpuscles in papillary dermis detect light touch and low-frequency stimuli.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q009.displayText: The marked structure is a Meissner corpuscle in the papillary dermis. It has a connective-tissue capsule and a stack of modified Schwann cells. These rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors are specialized for light touch and low-frequency stimuli and are abundant in sensitive glabrous skin.

rationales.a: Merkel cells are basal epidermal touch receptors, not the encapsulated corpuscle in papillary dermis.
rationales.c: Pacinian corpuscles are large, deep lamellar receptors for pressure/vibration; Meissner corpuscles are superficial and detect light touch.
rationales.d: Ruffini corpuscles are associated with skin stretch, not the rapidly adapting light-touch corpuscle in papillary dermis.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q010.takeaway: Panniculus adiposus is present in the axilla and absent in the scrotum, penis and eyelids.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q010.displayText: Panniculus adiposus is present in the axilla. It is a sheet of subcutaneous fat over most of the body and contributes to smooth skin contour. The source notes that it is absent in the scrotum, penis and eyelids.

rationales.b: The panniculus adiposus is absent in the scrotum, according to the source.
rationales.c: The eyelids are a source-listed site without panniculus adiposus.
rationales.d: The penis lacks panniculus adiposus in the source comparison.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q011.takeaway: The outer root sheath is glycogen-rich and appears clear on histology.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q011.displayText: The marked structure is the outer root sheath. From the hair shaft outward, the source describes medulla, cortex, inner root sheath, outer root sheath, glassy membrane and connective-tissue sheath. Cells of the outer root sheath appear clear because they contain glycogen.

rationales.a: The cuticle is the outermost layer of the hair shaft, not the glycogen-rich clear sheath around the follicle.
rationales.b: The medulla is the central part of the hair shaft.
rationales.c: The inner root sheath lies just inside the outer root sheath; the marked clear layer is the outer sheath.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q012.takeaway: Arrector pili are sympathetically innervated smooth muscles.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q012.displayText: Arrector pili are smooth muscles. They connect the undersurface of hair follicles to papillary dermis and are sympathetically innervated. Their contraction produces hair erection and goose flesh and helps squeeze sebaceous secretion into the follicle. The source notes their absence in several specialized hair regions.

rationales.a: Arrector pili is not skeletal muscle; it is an involuntary smooth-muscle bundle.
rationales.c: Arrector pili is smooth muscle only, not a mixture dominated by skeletal muscle.
rationales.d: The muscle is not mixed skeletal and smooth muscle; the arrector pili itself is smooth muscle.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q013.takeaway: Apocrine secretion releases product by shedding the apical part of a secretory cell.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q013.displayText: The schematic depicts an apocrine gland, in which the apical part of the secretory cell is shed during discharge. The source contrasts this with holocrine secretion, where the whole cell disintegrates, and merocrine secretion, where products are released by exocytosis while the cell remains intact.

rationales.a: Holocrine secretion destroys the whole cell, as in sebaceous glands; the image shows apical shedding.
rationales.b: Merocrine secretion releases product by exocytosis while the cell remains intact.
rationales.d: Endocrine cells release products into blood/interstitial fluid rather than shedding the apical part into a duct.

marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q014.takeaway: From anterior to posterior, the cornea has epithelium, Bowman layer, stroma, Descemet membrane and endothelium.
marrow__ANAT_CH16_Q014.displayText: X and Y are the corneal endothelium and Bowman's membrane, respectively. From anterior to posterior the source lists corneal epithelium, Bowman's layer, corneal stroma (substantia propria), Descemet's membrane and corneal endothelium. It also notes the recently described pre-Descemet/Dua layer between stroma and Descemet's membrane.

rationales.a: This places Bowman membrane before the anterior epithelium and misidentifies the posterior marker.
rationales.b: Descemet membrane is posterior to the stroma, while the marked anterior/posterior pair is endothelium and Bowman membrane.
rationales.d: Corneal epithelium and stroma are not the marked X/Y structures; the source key identifies endothelium and Bowman membrane.
